transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

I'm just having some trouble at work. Um, I'm a construction manager, and... well, I try to pay attention during safety briefings or plan reviews, but within a few minutes, my mind is just... off on three other job problems. I end up missing things I know I should have caught.

Do you notice this same difficulty concentrating in other areas of your life—like at home, during conversations with friends or family, or when doing things you enjoy—or is it mainly happening at work?

Yeah... I guess it happens other places, too. Like, my foreman, or my wife... they'll be talking straight to me, and I'm looking right at them. But then I have to stop them and say, uh, "Run that by me again." I just... I only ever catch the last few words.
How long have you been having these trouble focusing and paying attention? Has this been going on since you were younger, or did it start more recently?

Since I was a kid, I guess. Um... back in elementary school, my teachers were already telling my parents about it. Saying I wouldn't stay in my seat, or... talking out of turn. Losing my homework. They said I'd just rush through the directions before I even knew what they meant. So... yeah. It's not new.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F98.8, F41.1, F32.9, F33.9. Patient presents with lifelong history of inattention, impulsivity (rushing through directions), hyperactivity (not staying in seat, talking out of turn), and difficulty sustaining attention across multiple contexts (work, home, conversations). This is classic for ADHD, not anxiety disorder, generalized anxiety, major depressive disorder, or other specified behavioral disorder. The chronic onset since elementary school with persistent symptoms across settings is pathognomonic for ADHD.
